Note: Preferred template (survives editor review verbatim ~15x): 'Here the author/speaker is speaking as if X were Y. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use...' Keep this structure; do not over-explain.
Preferred template: 'The point of this comparison is that just as X, so is Y. If it would be helpful in your language, you could ...' Editors keep ~90% of simile notes in this form.
Preferred template: 'Here, **X** represents Y. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [...]' Editors keep ~87%.

Write only for genuinely abstract/theological ideas. Editors delete ~38% overall - especially notes on common nouns (tears, pain, life, violence, salvation, anger) and on repeated occurrences. Flag a given abstract noun once per passage, not every verse; later occurrences are covered by pipeline-generated see-how / also-occurs sentences.
Content-team mandate: every passive instance still gets a note - do not drop. Historical context only: editors deleted ~55% of these in LAM/HAB poetry before the mandate.
Only write when an antecedent is genuinely ambiguous across a clause boundary. Editors delete ~43%.
Skip for ordinary possessives; write only for non-ownership relations (e.g. 'daughter of Zion'). Editors delete ~61%.
Rarely worth a note in poetry; editors delete ~78%.
Only when the rhetorical force is not obvious to a modern reader. Editors delete ~42%.
Apply a high bar - editors delete ~50%; only supply implicit info a translator could not infer.
Genre-dependent: editors deleted 57% in HAB but kept all in LAM. Write only when the parallel line adds meaning, not for every poetic couplet.

Name notes should explain the significance or identity of the name, not merely label it. Editors consistently upgraded generic 'The word X is the name of a man/place' to notes that add meaning, e.g. 'Belteshazzar is the Babylonian name of Daniel' or 'Qoheleth is a title meaning one who assembles a group.' If the name has no useful significance, a note may still be omitted.
Context: translate-names — editors prefer explanatory over generic label

Note: STRENGTHEN (emphatic pronoun sub-type): In addition to ambiguous-referent cases, write a writing-pronouns note when an author states a pronoun explicitly even though the verb already encodes it — this is an emphatic construction signalling special focus. Editors across DAN, ZEC, and AMO consistently added notes for this pattern (e.g. 'I, Daniel' + verb that includes first-person). This is distinct from the ambiguous-referent case and survives at a higher rate.
Context: emphatic explicit-pronoun construction — added by editors

Note: STRENGTHEN (AT quality): When writing figs-activepassive alternate translations, always include at least one option that names the implied agent (God, a character, etc.), not only a generic active form. Editors consistently expanded single-option ATs by adding a named-agent alternative. E.g., instead of only [grew weak] also offer [God weakened them] or [someone pulled off its wings].

Chapter introductions should use a numbered structural outline (verse ranges + brief descriptors) rather than a prose paragraph summary of the chapter. Editors consistently replaced paragraph summaries with numbered outlines of 3-5 sections. Cultural/theological background should be given in separate headings after the outline. This pattern was observed across DAN, AMO, and 1CH intros.
Context: chapter intro format — numbered outline preferred over paragraph prose
